agent_3.question: Under what circumstances does the council decide to redistribute the reserve for scarcity or emergencies, and what criteria or process do they use to determine how the reserve is allocated?
agent_3.answer:
The council will decide to redistribute the communal reserve when the lake’s overall fish supply falls below a sustainable level, or when an emergency threatens the community’s food security.  In practice we look at two main triggers: 1) **Scarcity** – if the total catch for a season drops below roughly 70 % of the previous year’s average catch, or if the reserve itself is less than 1.5 kg (enough for only one fisherman to get his 1 kg minimum for two trips). 2) **Emergency** – a sudden event such as a drought, flood, disease outbreak or any situation that might suddenly increase food demand or cut off other sources.  When either trigger is reached, the council convenes a quick meeting (usually the next scheduled community gathering).  The council members review the current reserve level, the recent catch totals, and any reports of need.  A simple majority vote decides whether to redistribute.  If redistribution is approved, the reserve is divided either equally among all fishermen or, in the case of known extra hardship (e.g., a fisher who is ill or whose family is larger), allocated proportionally to need.  All transfers are logged in the communal ledger and the council’s treasurer records the amounts.  This process keeps the reserve useful for the whole village while ensuring fairness and accountability.

agent_1.question: What mechanism is in place to replenish the lake’s biomass if it falls below the 10% minimum?
agent_1.answer: If the lake’s biomass drops below the 10 % minimum, the lake will rely on its natural regeneration to get back up – fish reproduce, grow and new individuals enter the population each round.  In practice that means the ledger keeper will take any excess catch from a fisher that breached the rule and hold it in the community fish bank until the lake’s biomass can recover.  When the lake is below 10 % we can also decide to ban fishing for one round for that fisher, giving the lake time to rebound.  The bank can release fish that were held from previous excesses to help push the biomass back toward the 10 % floor.  So the mechanism is a combination of natural growth plus the fish bank’s buffer that is released when the lake’s stock is too low.

agent_1.question: What procedure does the ledger keeper use to determine and release fish from the community fish bank when the lake’s biomass falls below 10% to restore the minimum threshold?
agent_1.answer: The ledger keeper will check the lake’s total biomass after every round. If it’s below 10% of the lake’s pre‑round biomass, the keeper will calculate the shortfall – the amount needed to bring the lake back to that 10% minimum. That shortfall is taken from the community fish bank, which is stocked by the excess catch that earlier fishers were forced to deposit when they tried to take more than 10%. The keeper then releases that many kilos into the lake. If the bank doesn’t have enough to cover the deficit, the deficit remains and the keeper will enforce a one‑round fishing ban on any fisher whose catch contributed to the shortfall (i.e., those who exceeded 10% or whose catch pushed the lake below the 10% threshold). All of this is recorded on the Fish Ledger for transparency.

agent_2.question: When the council calculates 8 % of the lake’s current stock for the daily limit, at what point in the day is that stock measured, and how is the stock updated after each day’s harvest and after the communal pool’s contributions are added?
agent_2.answer: The council’s 8 % cap is taken from the lake’s stock **at the start of the fishing day**, before any nets are set.  At that moment the lake has a known amount, say S₀ kilograms.  The council calculates 0.08 × S₀ and that becomes the maximum total that may be taken that day.  All fish actually removed from the lake—whether the fisher keeps it or it is donated to the communal pool—count against that cap.  After the day’s harvest the lake’s stock is updated by subtracting the total weight caught (kept + donated).  The communal pool simply receives the donated weight; it does not alter the lake’s stock.  Thus on day n, if S₀ is the lake’s stock at the beginning, the end‑of‑day stock is S₁ = S₀ – T, where T is the total weight removed that day.  The pool grows by the donated portion of T, but the lake’s stock is lowered by the whole of T.

Thus the reduction persists until a round ends with the lake retaining at least 10 % of its biomass, at which point all fishers return to the 10 % allowance.

This procedure ensures that the 5 % reduction is a temporary, rule‑based penalty that automatically lifts when the lake’s health is restored.
